justification: Adds a gate over the table that is the product's differentiator, and the direction of risk is asymmetric: a FALSE EXPLANATION removes a real defect from the finding list permanently and silently, which is strictly worse than a false finding a human dismisses in a minute. Two live false-pass channels were found and closed during the work (clause references, numbered-list ordinals), so the risk is demonstrated, not theoretical.

falsifiable_check.passes_when: every one of the 1,069 controls is either derivable from its own source_text by a named rule, or already listed in scripts/control_source_values_baseline.json
falsifiable_check.fails_when: a control value no named rule derives is not in the baseline - either newly written, or an existing value edited to something its own quote no longer supports
falsifiable_check.demonstrated_failing: three ids removed from the baseline produced 'NEW (not in the baseline): 3' and exit code 1; restoring the baseline returned exit 0
falsifiable_check.mutation_evidence: three mutants injected into the rules, all three killed by tests/test_control_source_values.py: forcing the derived-value tolerance to always match, replacing exact numeric matching with a substring test, and letting the implied-rate rule fire when a numerator was written

pre_impl.schema_confirmed: value_min/value_max numeric (Decimal), source_text text and non-empty on all 1,069 rows, 83 rows carry no numeric value, 50 rows have min<>max, 18 distinct unit strings
pre_impl.population: all 1,069 rows, is_current deliberately unfiltered (989 current / 80 superseded) so the denominator reconciles with DQ-38 and link_controls_to_provisions.py; the split is selected and reported
pre_impl.timeout_risk: one read-only SELECT of 1,069 rows, no join, no batch loop - neither timeout nor loop-invariant applies

functions.name: explain_value
functions.input: one stored numeric value, the row's own quoted source_text, and the row's unit string so that unit-sensitive rules can refuse to fire
functions.output: the name of the first rule that derives the value from the text, paired with the exact substring that rule matched
functions.if_none: returns UNEXPLAINED with no evidence when no rule fires, and NO_VALUE_STORED when the value is absent or non-numeric or the quote is empty - three outcomes kept distinct, because 'nothing to check' is not 'checked and fine'

functions.name: explain_row
functions.input: one control row plus the names of its value columns, its source-text column and its unit column
functions.output: exactly one state for the row plus the per-field rule and evidence, so the printed counts always sum to the table size
functions.if_none: a row whose values are all absent becomes NO_VALUE_STORED rather than passing; a row with one unexplained end of a range becomes UNEXPLAINED even though its other end was explained

functions.name: _quantity_spans
functions.input: the raw source text of one control, which may contain clause references and numbered-list markers alongside real quantities
functions.output: value and character span for every number that is a quantity, with numbered-list ordinals removed
functions.if_none: text with no quantities yields an empty list, so the exact rule finds nothing and the row falls through to the derived rules rather than matching on a citation

functions.name: _rate_candidates
functions.input: the source text, scanned for every 'per N' / 'for every N' phrase and the numbers preceding each one
functions.output: every plausible numerator and denominator pair with its evidence, nearest numerator first, stopping at a sentence or table-cell break
functions.if_none: yields a None numerator when nothing numeric precedes the rate, which is the signal the implied-unity rule uses to decide whether assuming 1 is safe

values.name: UNEXPLAINED
values.meaning: no named rule derives the stored number from the row's own quoted source_text - this is the finding, not an error state
values.not: it does NOT mean the number is wrong; it means nothing in the quote supports it, which is a question for a human against the source PDF

values.name: no_value_stored
values.meaning: the row records a control with no number at all (83 rows) - counted as its own state
values.not: deliberately NOT counted as a pass; folding it into the explained bucket would overstate the pass rate by about 8 percentage points

queries.sql: SELECT id, lga, control_type, dev_type, value_min, value_max, unit, source_text, section_ref, condition, extraction_method, is_current FROM dcp_setback_controls ORDER BY lga, control_type, id
queries.filters: none, deliberately: filtering is_current would shrink the denominator away from DQ-38's 1,069 and stop the two scripts reconciling. is_current is selected and the split reported instead.

break_it: A rule fires on a number inside a clause reference: 's4.3.6' would let a stored 4.3 explain itself by its own citation. Closed by lookarounds on the number token; it cost 5 rows their explanation.

A rule fires on a numbered-list ordinal: Camden control 693 stored a 2.0 m front setback and was explained by the '2' of a list item, in a clause about front FENCE height. Closed by excluding list ordinals from quantity matching.
The implied-unity rate rule explains '2 spaces per 5 dwellings' stored as 0.2 as if it were 1/5. Closed by refusing to fire when any numerator was written.
A percentage rule divides any number by 100 until something matches. Closed by requiring a literal '%' or 'per cent' adjacent to the number.
The nil rule reads City of Sydney's 'where no front setback is shown on the map' as a control of zero. Closed by requiring the word 'required'; a map being silent is not a control.

An over-tight number lookahead rejected a number ending a sentence ('Maximum: up to 3.') and manufactured findings out of correct rows. Caught by re-reading the residue, fixed, and covered by a regression test.
One end of a range is explained and the other is not. explain_row marks the whole row unexplained: a range whose upper bound came from nowhere is not a verified range.
post_merge: The 25 baselined rows are real data defects and are NOT fixed by this PR. Each needs a ruling against the source PDF. The four Waverley deep-soil rows (10%/15% against a quote saying 50%) and the three Cumberland setbacks (4.0/5.5/8.0 m against a quote whose only figure is 6m) are the ones to take first.

fabricated_values does not catch 'needs PDF verification' - its marker pattern has 'to be verified' but not this wording, which is why controls 1119 and 1120 store a number against a quote admitting it is unverified.
